quote: Should he come near me, I could not answer him.
firstReading: Job acknowledges God’s incomparable majesty and the frailty of any human attempt to contend with him. The Lord acts with sovereign power over earth, sea, and stars; his deeds exceed human comprehension, and he may pass by without being perceived. Even one convinced of innocence cannot place God under judgment, but can only appeal to his mercy.
psalmSummary: Psalm 88 gives voice to a sufferer who feels near death and abandoned in darkness. The psalmist asks whether the dead can proclaim God’s wonders, mercy, fidelity, and saving justice. Rather than concealing anguish, this prayer brings its piercing questions directly before the Lord, continuing to seek him amid affliction.
gospelSummary: As Jesus journeys onward, he clarifies the uncompromising character of discipleship. To one eager follower, he reveals that the Son of Man has no settled place of rest. To another, he gives priority to proclaiming the Kingdom over even a weighty family obligation. A third is warned that discipleship cannot be divided by continual backward-looking attachment. Jesus does not dismiss love for family or the reality of grief; rather, he declares that his call and the Kingdom demand an undivided heart. Those who follow him must receive his path of poverty, urgency, and resolute fidelity.
saintReflection: Saint Jerome (Memorial): Saint Jerome (c. 347–420), priest and Doctor of the Church, devoted his life to the study, translation, and interpretation of Sacred Scripture. After study in Rome and periods of ascetical life in the East, he settled at Bethlehem, where prayer and sustained attention to Hebrew and Greek informed his biblical work. His translations and revisions became foundational to the Latin Vulgate. Jerome insisted that Scripture should be read within the faith of the Church and allowed to shape conduct, not merely satisfy intellectual curiosity. His conviction that 'ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ' expresses the intimate relation between the biblical word and knowledge of the incarnate Word. His own difficult temperament also shows why learning must be accompanied by continual conversion. Reflection on Jerome invites reverent study, prayerful listening, humility in interpretation, and a willingness to live what God's word reveals.
dailyPrayer:
Lord God, you are great beyond all measure, and your ways surpass the limits of my understanding. When suffering, uncertainty, or hiddenness make prayer difficult, keep me from turning away from you. Receive the questions and grief that I cannot resolve, as you received the cry of the psalmist.

Jesus Christ, make my heart ready to follow you without reserve. Free me from attachments that hinder obedience to your Kingdom, from delay when you call me to charity, and from the temptation to look back rather than walk in your way. Teach me to accept your poverty and to seek first the proclamation of your saving reign.

Through the intercession of Saint Jerome, grant me reverence for Sacred Scripture. Give me diligence to hear your word within the faith of the Church, humility to receive its correction, and grace to put it into practice. May your word lead me more deeply into knowledge and love of you, who live and reign forever. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
Job, the psalmist, and the disciples in Luke stand before the mystery of God, whose presence cannot be mastered or managed. Job confesses that the Creator’s wisdom exceeds every human claim. Psalm 88 shows that this confession does not silence lament: faith may ask why God seems distant while still addressing him as Lord. In Christ, God’s mysterious transcendence draws near in a person who calls disciples to accompany him.

Jesus’ call is definitive because the Kingdom is present in him. His poverty, homelessness, and journeying toward Jerusalem disclose the form of messianic obedience. To follow him is not simply to admire his teaching, but to let his Kingdom reorder every allegiance. This does not despise created goods or family duties; it establishes that no good can replace obedience to the Lord.

Saint Jerome directs the Church to meet this demanding word through prayerful, ecclesial reading. Scripture reveals both God’s majesty and Christ’s summons. The reader is not its judge. Humbly received, the word exposes hesitation, consoles honest sorrow, and forms a heart capable of persevering after Christ.
exegesis:
Context: Job 9 belongs to Job’s reply after he has heard claims that suffering can be readily explained by human guilt and divine recompense. Job does not deny God’s justice; indeed, he begins by admitting that no mortal can be righteous before God in the sense of successfully entering a lawsuit against him. The issue is not whether God lacks justice, but whether a suffering person can comprehend or litigate the divine governance of the world. Job’s language is deliberately overwhelming. God overturns mountains, shakes the earth, commands the sun, and orders the constellations. The Creator’s acts cannot be circumscribed by human scrutiny. He may move near, yet remain unseen. Job therefore describes not unbelief but the painful condition of creaturely limitation before the holy God.

Context: The omitted verses are important to the movement of the passage, but the verses proclaimed press the central point: even if Job were able to answer, he would not stand as God’s equal. He could only plead for mercy. This is not a denial of the reality of Job’s pain or of the questions raised by his affliction. Rather, it rejects the presumption that a creature can compel God to give an account according to creaturely standards. Christian faith receives this truth while also confessing that God is not remote from human misery. The God whose wisdom surpasses us has acted in history and, in the fullness of time, has spoken through his Son. Job’s reverent perplexity prepares the hearer to seek God humbly rather than to reduce him to an explanation.

Psalm: Psalm 88 is one of Scripture’s starkest prayers of lament. Its questions concerning death do not offer a detached account of the state of the dead; they give expression to someone who fears that affliction will end praise, communion, and the public proclamation of God’s saving deeds. The psalmist asks whether God’s wonders, mercy, faithfulness, and justice can be known in the realm of darkness. Yet the very asking is an act of faith. The sufferer does not address emptiness but the God whose steadfast love and fidelity he knows. The prayer teaches the Church that anguish need not be disguised before God. Honest lament can remain prayer when it turns toward the Lord, even where consolation has not yet appeared.

Gospel: Luke places these encounters as Jesus travels with resolute purpose. The first person volunteers to follow him wherever he goes. Jesus answers by identifying the cost of joining his way: animals have places of shelter, but the Son of Man does not claim such security. His mission does not proceed by ordinary settledness; it moves toward the Paschal mystery. The second encounter makes the urgency even sharper. The command to follow is answered with a request connected to burial of a father, an obligation of profound seriousness. Jesus’ response establishes that the announcement of God’s Kingdom has decisive priority. The saying is not contempt for the dead or a repeal of the duty to honor parents. It reveals that when Christ calls, even sacred obligations cannot become a reason for refusing the one through whom the Kingdom comes.

Gospel: The final saying uses the image of plowing. A furrow cannot be properly made by someone who persistently turns around; similarly, discipleship cannot flourish in a heart that attempts to follow Christ while continually reserving itself for what has been left behind. Jesus calls for a whole-hearted orientation toward the Kingdom. Luke’s Gospel will show that this is not achieved by human force alone. It is Christ who goes ahead toward his saving death and resurrection, and it is his grace that creates perseverance in his followers. The Gospel therefore confronts every partial response: admiration without obedience, intention without readiness, and attachment to former securities that resists the road on which the Lord leads.

Saints: Saint Jerome is a fitting witness on this memorial because he devoted his life to the study, translation, and interpretation of Sacred Scripture. His labor among the biblical languages was joined to prayer and ascetical discipline, not separated from them. The readings require precisely this reverent manner of hearing. Job cannot be treated as a simple solution to suffering, Psalm 88 cannot be silenced because its grief is severe, and Jesus’ words cannot be softened until they ask nothing of the hearer. Jerome’s insistence that Scripture belongs within the faith of the Church guards against making the biblical word serve private preference. His life also recalls that knowledge must be accompanied by conversion: the word is received truly when it reforms conduct and draws the reader toward Christ.

Today: The Church hears these texts as an invitation to humility, truthful prayer, and decisive obedience. Before God’s mysterious wisdom, believers need not pretend to possess answers to every sorrow. With Job, they acknowledge the Creator’s greatness; with the psalmist, they bring their darkness into prayer; with the disciples, they hear Christ’s call anew. Study of Scripture, especially in the spirit commended by Saint Jerome, is not merely the gathering of information. It is attentive listening to the living God who addresses his people. The proper fruit is a heart less occupied with judging God’s ways, more willing to lament faithfully, and more ready to follow Jesus wherever the proclamation of his Kingdom leads.
